              The Use of Recovery Strategies in Professional Soccer:
                              A Worldwide Survey
                   Adam Field, Liam D. Harper, Bryna C.R. Chrismas, Peter M. Fowler, Alan McCall,
                                   Darren J. Paul, Karim Chamari, and Lee Taylor

     Purpose: To survey soccer practitioners’ recovery strategy: (1) use, (2) perceived effectiveness, and (3) factors inﬂuencing their
     implementation in professional soccer. Methods: A cross-sectional convenience sample of professional soccer club/confederation
     practitioners completed a web-based survey (April to July 2020). Pearson chi-square and Fisher exact tests with Cramer V (φ − c)
     assessed relationships and their strength, respectively, between the perceived effectiveness and frequency of strategy use. Results: A
     total of 80 soccer practitioners (13 countries) completed the survey. The 3 most important recovery objectives were “alleviating muscle
     damage/fatigue,” “minimizing injury risk,” and “performance optimization.” The most frequently used strategies were active recovery,
     structured recovery day, extra rest day, massage, cold-water therapy, and carbohydrate provision (predominantly on match day and
     match day + 1). Relationships were identiﬁed between perceived effectiveness and frequency of strategy use for sleep medication
     (P < .001, φ − c = 0.48), carbohydrate provision (P = .007, φ − c = 0.60), protein provision (P = .007, φ − c = 0.63), an extra rest day
     (P < .001, φ − c = 0.56), and a structured recovery day (P = .049, φ − c = 0.50). Conclusions: The study demonstrates that professional
     soccer practitioners have a range of objectives geared toward enhancing player recovery. A disconnect is apparent between the
     perceived effectiveness of many recovery strategies and their frequency of use in an applied setting. Novel data indicate that strategies
     are most frequently employed around match day. Challenges to strategy adoption are mainly competing disciplinary interests and
     resource limitations. Researchers and practitioners should liaise to ensure that the complexities involved with operating in an applied
     environment are elucidated and apposite study designs are adopted, in turn, facilitating the use of practically effective and compatible
     recovery modalities.

     Keywords: football, practitioner, coach, applied practice, qualitative research

 "decision":"INCLUDE",

 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The Strengthen your ankle program to prevent recurrent injuries: A randomized controlled trial aimed at long-term effectiveness' matches the filename.",

 "studyDesign":"Randomized Controlled Trial",

 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Athletic Training","Sports Medicine","Rehabilitation"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified","Male Athletes","Female Athletes","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A randomised controlled trial with 12 months of follow-up in 220 athletes aged 18 to 70 who had an ankle sprain in the two months before enrolment. Participants were randomised to an 8-week neuromuscular training program delivered by a free smartphone app (n=110) or a printed booklet (n=110). Recurrent self-reported ankle sprains did not differ between groups (incidence density 15.59 vs 15.84 per 1000 h; HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.49), and median FADI scores rose by similar amounts in both groups with no significant between-group differences at any month.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Recurrence was self-reported, and compliance was assumed equal rather than measured over the 12-month follow-up. The sample was sized for 8-week compliance, not long-term injury outcomes, so the study may lack power for differences in recurrence. The time-loss hazard ratio in Table 2 (0.55, CI 0.82 to 1.09) is internally inconsistent because the point estimate lies outside its interval.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the null result as showing that an app and a booklet are interchangeable for injury prevention in general, when the trial only compared two delivery methods of one program under an assumption of equal compliance.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2017,
   "citation":"Van Reijen M, Vriend I, Zuidema V, van Mechelen W, Verhagen EA. The “Strengthen your ankle” program to prevent recurrent injuries: A randomized controlled trial aimed at long-term effectiveness. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2017;20:549-554.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.jsams.2016.12.001",
   "abstract":"In a 12-month randomised trial of 220 athletes with a recent ankle sprain, delivering the same neuromuscular training program by app or printed booklet produced similar rates of recurrent ankle sprains and similar improvement in ankle function scores. The authors conclude the two delivery methods are similarly effective when compliance is equal during the 8-week program.",
   "tldr":"For athletes recovering from an ankle sprain, a free app and a printed booklet delivering the same 8-week program led to similar rates of recurrent sprain over a year. The result depends on compliance being equal, which the study did not measure over the follow-up.",
   "methods":"Randomised controlled trial with 12-month follow-up in 220 athletes (18 to 70 years) recruited from October 2013 to April 2014, with recent ankle sprain as an inclusion criterion. Participants were randomised to the Strengthen your ankle app (n=110) or a printed booklet (n=110) with the same six exercises, three sessions per week for 8 weeks. Monthly online questionnaires collected sports exposure, self-reported recurrences and FADI scores. Incidence density per 1000 h was analysed with Cox regression, and FADI with Mann-Whitney U tests, on an intention-to-treat basis.",
   "findings":"Self-reported recurrences were 70 in the app group and 69 in the booklet group (incidence density 15.59 vs 15.84 per 1000 h; HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.49). Injuries leading to time loss and to costs did not differ significantly. Median FADI rose from 92.9 to 100 in the app group and from 93.8 to 100 in the booklet group, with no significant between-group difference at any month. Cumulative recurrences per participant did not differ significantly between groups.",
   "limitations":"Self-reported outcomes with no objective confirmation of sprains. Compliance was measured only during the 8-week intervention, and the authors assume equal compliance afterwards. The sample size was calculated from expected compliance rather than long-term injury rates, so power to detect long-term differences is limited. Table 2 gives a time-loss HR of 0.55 with a CI of 0.82 to 1.09, which does not contain its own estimate, so that row should be checked against the source. Participation in the trial may have influenced continued use of either method.",
   "practicalImplications":"Either an app or a printed booklet can deliver this neuromuscular program, so the choice can follow local access and athlete preference. The study does not show that either format keeps athletes exercising for a year, so staff should still monitor adherence.",
   "athleteDev":"The trial tests delivery methods for an injury-prevention program, not performance outcomes, so it offers no basis for changing performance training. Its relevance to athlete development is limited to how prevention exercises are delivered.",
   "rtp":"Athletes in the trial were recruited within two months of a sprain, and the program was used as a preventive measure rather than a return-to-sport protocol. The study cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria, although the FADI results describe ongoing pain and disability after sprain."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q49",
 "sourceFile":"The use of recovery strategies in professional soccer - A worldwide survey.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The Use of Recovery Strategies in Professional Soccer: A Worldwide Survey' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Soccer"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A cross-sectional web survey of 80 soccer practitioners from 13 countries (April to July 2020), mainly science and medical staff, about which recovery strategies their teams use, on which days of the microcycle, how effective they rate them (1 to 10), and what limits use. Active recovery, structured recovery days, extra rest days and carbohydrate and protein provision were the most used strategies. Perceived effectiveness and frequency of use were associated for sleep medication, carbohydrate, protein, extra rest day and structured recovery day (P <= .049), but not for most other strategies.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The data are a convenience sample of one response per team, with uneven representation of roles and leagues, and the authors ran no inferential comparisons between groups. The data describe practitioner perceptions and reported use, not athlete recovery outcomes or the effectiveness of any strategy.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the perceived-effectiveness ratings as evidence that strategies such as carbohydrate or protein provision improve recovery, when the survey measured practitioners' views rather than outcomes.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Field A, Harper LD, Chrismas BCR, Fowler PM, McCall A, Paul DJ, Chamari K, Taylor L. The Use of Recovery Strategies in Professional Soccer: A Worldwide Survey. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2021 (ahead of print).",
   "doi":"10.1123/ijspp.2020-0799",
   "abstract":"A web survey of 80 professional soccer practitioners in 13 countries described which recovery strategies they use, when in the week they use them, how effective they rate them, and what stops them using others. The most used strategies were active recovery, structured recovery days, extra rest days, massage and cold-water therapy, and frequency of use matched perceived effectiveness for only a few strategies.",
   "tldr":"Soccer staff mostly use recovery strategies around match day and rate several of them highly, yet many highly rated strategies are used infrequently. Competing staff interests and limited resources are the main barriers.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional convenience survey of soccer practitioners, April to July 2020, with 80 complete responses out of 100 received. The survey covered objectives, use by day of the microcycle (MD-3 to MD+3), perceived effectiveness on a 1 to 10 scale, and open-ended barriers. Descriptive statistics, Pearson chi-square and Fisher exact tests with Cramer's V assessed associations between perceived effectiveness and use.",
   "findings":"The three most important recovery objectives were alleviating muscle damage or fatigue, minimising injury risk, and performance optimisation. Most teams used active recovery (97%), structured recovery days (94%), extra rest days (94%), carbohydrate provision (90%) and protein provision (85%). Associations between perceived effectiveness and frequency of use were significant for sleep medication (P < .001, Cramer's V 0.48), carbohydrate (P = .007, 0.60), protein (P = .007, 0.63), extra rest day (P < .001, 0.56) and structured recovery day (P = .049, 0.50). Most strategies were used most often on MD or MD+1.",
   "limitations":"Convenience sample with one response per team, unequal representation of roles and leagues (32 science, 33 medical and 15 coaching staff), and no inferential comparison between groups. Data were collected during 2020 and reflect a single-week microcycle that may not match two- or three-game weeks. The survey did not measure athlete outcomes, and some questions (such as those on sleep) may have been interpreted differently by respondents.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff can compare their own day-by-day use of recovery strategies with the pattern reported here, which shows most strategies used around match day and the day after. The survey cannot show which strategies improve recovery, so the high ratings should not be taken as evidence of benefit.",
   "athleteDev":"The survey describes how recovery strategies are scheduled across a soccer microcycle and the barriers to using them. It does not test whether any strategy changes performance, so it cannot justify a performance training prescription.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveys practitioners about routine recovery use in players, not injured athletes or return-to-play protocols."
 }
}

16	Abstract
17	Background Technology has long been used to track player movements in team sports, with initial tracking via manual coding
18	of video footage. Since then, wearable microtechnology in the form of global and local positioning systems has provided a less
19	labour-intensive way of monitoring movements. As such, there has been a proliferation in research pertaining to these devices.
20	Objective A systematic review of studies that investigate the validity and/or reliability of wearable microtechnology to
21	quantify movement and specific actions common to intermittent team sports.
22	Methods A systematic search of CINAHL, MEDLINE, and SPORTDiscus was performed; studies included must have been
23	(1) original research investigations; (2) full-text articles written in English; (3) published in a peer-reviewed academic jour-
24	nal; and (4) assessed the validity and/or reliability of wearable microtechnology to quantify movements or specific actions
25	common to intermittent team sports.
26	Results A total of 384 studies were retrieved and 187 were duplicates. The titles and abstracts of 197 studies were screened
27	and the full texts of 88 manuscripts were assessed. A total of 62 studies met the inclusion criteria. Additional 10 studies,
28	identified via reference list assessment, were included. Therefore, a total of 72 studies were included in this review.
29	Conclusion There are many studies investigating the validity and reliability of wearable microtechnology to track movement
30	and detect sport-specific actions. It is evident that for the majority of metrics, validity and reliability are multi-factorial, in that
31	it is dependent upon a wide variety of factors including wearable technology brand and model, sampling rate, type of move-
32	ment performed (e.g., straight line, change of direction) and intensity of movement (e.g., walk, sprint). Practitioners should
33	be mindful of the accuracy and repeatability of the devices they are using when making decisions on player training loads.

    SYSTEMATIC REVIEW



The Validity and Reliability of Wearable Microtechnology
for Intermittent Team Sports: A Systematic Review
Zachary L. Crang1 · Grant Duthie2 · Michael H. Cole1 · Jonathon Weakley1,3 · Adam Hewitt1 · Rich D. Johnston1,3

Accepted: 28 November 2020
© Crown 2020


Abstract
Background Technology has long been used to track player movements in team sports, with initial tracking via manual coding
of video footage. Since then, wearable microtechnology in the form of global and local positioning systems has provided a less
labour-intensive way of monitoring movements. As such, there has been a proliferation in research pertaining to these devices.
Objective A systematic review of studies that investigate the validity and/or reliability of wearable microtechnology to
quantify movement and specific actions common to intermittent team sports.
Methods A systematic search of CINAHL, MEDLINE, and SPORTDiscus was performed; studies included must have been
(1) original research investigations; (2) full-text articles written in English; (3) published in a peer-reviewed academic jour-
nal; and (4) assessed the validity and/or reliability of wearable microtechnology to quantify movements or specific actions
common to intermittent team sports.
Results A total of 384 studies were retrieved and 187 were duplicates. The titles and abstracts of 197 studies were screened
and the full texts of 88 manuscripts were assessed. A total of 62 studies met the inclusion criteria. Additional 10 studies,
identified via reference list assessment, were included. Therefore, a total of 72 studies were included in this review.
Conclusion There are many studies investigating the validity and reliability of wearable microtechnology to track movement
and detect sport-specific actions. It is evident that for the majority of metrics, validity and reliability are multi-factorial, in that
it is dependent upon a wide variety of factors including wearable technology brand and model, sampling rate, type of move-
ment performed (e.g., straight line, change of direction) and intensity of movement (e.g., walk, sprint). Practitioners should
be mindful of the accuracy and repeatability of the devices they are using when making decisions on player training loads.

 "sourceFile":"The validity and reliability of wearable microtechnology for intermittent team sports - A systematic review.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",

 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The Validity and Reliability of Wearable Microtechnology for Intermittent Team Sports: A Systematic Review' matches the filename.",

 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Research & Analytics","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A PRISMA systematic review of CINAHL, MEDLINE and SPORTDiscus, with reference-list searching, identifying 72 peer-reviewed studies of the validity and/or reliability of GNSS, local positioning and inertial devices for team sport movement (62 from the database search, 10 from reference lists). Quality scores on a modified Downs and Black checklist ranged from 64% to 100% (mean 86.4%). Validity and reliability depended on device brand, sampling rate, movement type and intensity: 10 Hz or higher GNSS was generally more accurate and reliable than 5 Hz or 1 Hz devices, and LPS accuracy fell when set-up was sub-optimal or when change of direction was repeated.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The studies were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis, so the findings are narrative and count-based. Many criterion measures were timing gates or tape measures rather than gold-standard 3D motion capture, and intra-device reliability could not be separated from biological variation.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the review as clearing all wearable devices for load decisions, when accuracy depends on the specific device, sampling rate, set-up and movement type, and many metrics have only a few studies.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Crang ZL, Duthie G, Cole MH, Weakley J, Hewitt A, Johnston RD. The Validity and Reliability of Wearable Microtechnology for Intermittent Team Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2020.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-020-01399-1",
   "abstract":"This systematic review of 72 studies found that the validity and reliability of GNSS, local positioning and inertial wearable devices in team sports depend on the brand, sampling rate, movement type and intensity. Practitioners should consider device accuracy and repeatability when making training load decisions.",
   "tldr":"Wearable GPS and tracking data are only as good as the specific device, sampling rate and movement being measured. Devices at 10 Hz or above were generally more accurate and reliable than 1 or 5 Hz units, and many metrics have too few studies to trust.",
   "methods":"PRISMA systematic review (March 2020 search) of SPORTDiscus, CINAHL and MEDLINE for English-language peer-reviewed studies of validity and/or reliability of wearable microtechnology for intermittent team sport movement. Two authors screened records and extracted data; quality was scored on a modified Downs and Black checklist. Results were summarised narratively by metric, device and study type because of heterogeneity.",
   "findings":"72 studies were included: 384 records retrieved, 187 duplicates removed, 88 full texts assessed, 62 included plus 10 from reference lists. GNSS was generally valid for total distance in continuous and team sport movements, but 1 Hz and 5 Hz devices were less accurate for short straight-line and direction-change movements. For peak velocity, GNSS was generally accurate in straight-line sprinting. Between-device reliability was better for 10 Hz and above, and 5 Hz devices showed poor reliability for high-intensity accelerations. LPS was accurate for distance when set up correctly, but errors rose to 15 to 30% bias under sub-optimal set-up and with repeated change of direction. Intra-device reliability was poorly studied because identical movements cannot be repeated.",
   "limitations":"Narrative synthesis only, with heterogeneous methods and devices. Many validity studies used timing gates, tape measures or radar rather than gold-standard 3D motion capture, and several metrics were based on a single device or system. Intra-device reliability values mix biological and technological variation. Only English-language journal articles from three databases were searched, and the search ended in March 2020.",
   "practicalImplications":"Practitioners should check the sampling rate, set-up and movement type behind any device metric before using it for training load decisions. Devices at 10 Hz or above are the safer choice for distance and high-speed measures, and comparisons between players should use devices of the same type. The review does not provide thresholds for individual decisions.",
   "athleteDev":"Training load tracking is only as reliable as the device and metric used, so performance staff should interpret speed, distance and acceleration data within the device error before prescribing top-up sessions or progressing training. The review does not test performance outcomes.",
   "rtp":"The review covers device accuracy in healthy team sport movement and cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It does note that device error should be accounted for when rehabilitation loads are increased using speed and distance data."
 }
}

content.content:
prolympic sports including lucrative sponsorships, financial gain for some elite athletes, increased
social status via high profile media exposure, and sports funding strategies both at the organizational
and U.S. national levels that rewarded high performers and punished, or eliminated nonperformers.
Other influential factors were also discussed including the emergence of new sports norms related to
advances in sport medicine, technology and training methods, and the related increase in the
availability of performance enhancing substances for use as training and recovery aides, and in
competition. Another important omission not specifically mentioned by Coakley included the adop­
tion of worldwide, legal statutes regarding prohibited doping substances and methods.
    This article does not surmount the central limitation of H&C’s original article. It does not
empirically test either their original model, or an alternative model of performance enhancing
substance and methods (PESM) use. However, an effort is made in this paper to account theoretically
for many of the emergent factors that have limited the validity of the central arguments made in
H&C’s original work as they relate to PESM use in sport over time. Despite the critical tone of this
paper, it is important to state that the central aim is not a complete discounting of H&C’s positive
deviance/overconformity model as it applies to the use of PESM among some individual athletes. It is
also important to point out that the H&C model can be used to validly and reliably explain other types
of deviant non-PESM behavior among athletes.
    The primary objective of this paper is to demonstrate that the validity of the H&C model of
deviance as it applies to PESM use is context specific and depends on the time, place, social groups
involved (Thio 1983), and the relative power of the audience and deviant(s) (Heckert and Heckert
2002, Thio 1983). It is recognized that the H&C model may have more explanatory power in the
contextualize and understand them all.
   Finally, it is also important to point to an additional nuance concerning the contextual relevance of
deviance in general. While PESM use behavior may be understood as a form of overconformity that is
positively/negatively evaluated in one sport context, it may often simultaneously be understood as
a form of underconformity in another and is subsequently evaluated differently. Reactive under­
standing of deviant PESM behavior may also evolve among athletes (Brissonneau and Ohl 2010) and
other sports stakeholders over time. Power relations between social actors determine which view is
most accepted within and between social contexts. Research that is motivated by a broader conception
of deviant PESM use behavior is well positioned to identify and explain both varied and nuanced
PESM behavior that has been increasingly found in contemporary sport. Adopting this orientation is
also likely to move PESM future research beyond the simplistic dichotomy of PESM behavior as either
negatively/positively deviant. At the same time, using H&H’s more complete synthetic theoretical
approach can help to resolve some of the seemingly divergent/contradictory findings on PESM use
between and within fields. A future line of research informed by this broader framework could also
help to determine which type/s of deviant PESM behavior is/are most prevalent and how it/they
change over time.


Acknowledgements
I would like to thank the three reviewers for their useful recommendations and clear editorial remarks.

20	                                      Context: Hamstring strain is a common injury to the lower limbs. Early intervention in the acute phase aids with restoring
21	                                      hamstring function and prevents secondary related injury.
22	                                      Objective: To systematically review and summarize the effectiveness of exercise-based interventions combined with
23	                                      physical modalities currently used in athletes with acute hamstring injuries.
24	                                      Data Sources: Five databases (EMBASE, Medline, Cochrane Library, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science) were searched
25	                                      from inception to July 2021.
26	                                      Study Selection: A total of 4569 studies were screened. Nine randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on the effect of
27	                                      therapeutic exercise programs with and without physical agents in athletes with acute hamstring injuries were identified for
28	                                      meta-analysis.
29	                                      Study Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis
30	                                      Level of Evidence: Level 1
31	                                      Data Extraction: The studies were screened, and the evidence was rated using the PEDro scale. Nine RCTs with PEDro
32	                                      scores ranging between 3 and 9 were included and extracted pain intensity, time to return to play (TTRTP), and reinjury rate
33	                                      in the study.
34	                                      Results: Loading exercises during extensive lengthening were shown to facilitate TTRTP at P < 0.0001 but did not prevent
35	                                      recurrence (P = 0.17), whereas strengthening with trunk stabilization and agility exercise did not reduce the duration of
36	                                      injury recurrence (P = 0.16), but significantly reduced the reinjury rate (P < 0.007) at a 12-month follow-up.
37	                                      The results of the stretching programs and solely physical modalities could not be pooled in the statistical analysis.
38	                                      Conclusion: The meta-analysis indicated that a loading program helps athletes to return to sports on a timely basis.
39	                                      Although strengthening with trunk stabilization and agility exercise cannot significantly reduce recovery time, the program
40	                                      can prevent reinjury. The clinical effects of stretching programs and pure physical modality interventions could not be
41	                                      concluded in this study due to limited evidence.
42	                                      PROSPERO Registration: CRD42020183035
43	                                      Keywords: acute hamstring injuries; pain; physical modalities; therapeutic exercise; time to return to play; reinjury rate

                                      Therapeutic Exercises and Modalities in
                                      Athletes With Acute Hamstring Injuries:
                                      A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
                                      Amornthep Jankaew, MSc,† Jih-Ching Chen, MSc,‡ Samatchai Chamnongkich, PhD, PT,§
                                      and Cheng-Feng Lin, PhD, PT†‡||*


                                      Context: Hamstring strain is a common injury to the lower limbs. Early intervention in the acute phase aids with restoring
                                      hamstring function and prevents secondary related injury.
                                      Objective: To systematically review and summarize the effectiveness of exercise-based interventions combined with
                                      physical modalities currently used in athletes with acute hamstring injuries.
                                      Data Sources: Five databases (EMBASE, Medline, Cochrane Library, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science) were searched
                                      from inception to July 2021.
                                      Study Selection: A total of 4569 studies were screened. Nine randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on the effect of
                                      therapeutic exercise programs with and without physical agents in athletes with acute hamstring injuries were identified for
                                      meta-analysis.
                                      Study Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis
                                      Level of Evidence: Level 1
                                      Data Extraction: The studies were screened, and the evidence was rated using the PEDro scale. Nine RCTs with PEDro
                                      scores ranging between 3 and 9 were included and extracted pain intensity, time to return to play (TTRTP), and reinjury rate
                                      in the study.
                                      Results: Loading exercises during extensive lengthening were shown to facilitate TTRTP at P < 0.0001 but did not prevent
                                      recurrence (P = 0.17), whereas strengthening with trunk stabilization and agility exercise did not reduce the duration of
                                      injury recurrence (P = 0.16), but significantly reduced the reinjury rate (P < 0.007) at a 12-month follow-up.
                                      The results of the stretching programs and solely physical modalities could not be pooled in the statistical analysis.
                                      Conclusion: The meta-analysis indicated that a loading program helps athletes to return to sports on a timely basis.
                                      Although strengthening with trunk stabilization and agility exercise cannot significantly reduce recovery time, the program
                                      can prevent reinjury. The clinical effects of stretching programs and pure physical modality interventions could not be
                                      concluded in this study due to limited evidence.
                                      PROSPERO Registration: CRD42020183035
                                      Keywords: acute hamstring injuries; pain; physical modalities; therapeutic exercise; time to return to play; reinjury rate

Strengthening with trunk stabilisation and agility did not significantly change time to return to play (mean difference -3.78 days, P = 0.16) but lowered 12-month reinjury (risk difference -0.41, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.11, two trials).",

 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the earlier return to play with loading as a general rule for all hamstring injuries, when the pooled evidence comes from two trials in elite football players and sprinters or jumpers using eccentric lengthening loads.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,

   "doi":"10.1177/19417381221118085",
   "abstract":"In nine randomised trials of 396 athletes with acute hamstring injuries, a loading program during extensive lengthening shortened time to return to play compared with a conventional program. Strengthening with trunk stabilisation and agility reduced reinjury at 12 months but did not significantly shorten time to return to play, and the evidence on stretching and physical modalities was too limited to pool.",
   "tldr":"For athletes with acute hamstring injuries, eccentric loading during lengthening was linked with a faster return to play, and strengthening with trunk and agility work was linked with fewer reinjuries at 12 months. The evidence rests on few small trials, mostly in male athletes.",
   "methods":"Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA and the Cochrane Handbook, with five databases searched from inception to July 2021 and registration on PROSPERO. Included studies were RCTs of exercise-based or physical-modality treatment in athletes with acute hamstring injuries. Quality was rated with the PEDro scale, and outcomes (time to return to play, pain and reinjury rate) were pooled with fixed or random effects models in RevMan.",
   "findings":"Nine RCTs were included from 24 full texts assessed. Loading during lengthening versus conventional exercise: time to return to play was 28.29 days shorter (mean difference -28.29, 95% CI -41.60 to -14.99, P < 0.0001), and reinjury did not differ (risk difference -0.05, P = 0.17). Strengthening with trunk stabilisation and agility versus other programs: time to return to play did not differ (mean difference -3.78 days, 95% CI -9.04 to 1.48, P = 0.16), reinjury at 6 months did not differ (risk difference -0.00, P = 0.97), and at 12 months reinjury was lower (risk difference -0.41, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.11, P < 0.007, two studies). Stretching programs and physical modalities could not be pooled.",
   "limitations":"Nine small RCTs with 396 participants, 93.7% male, and quality scores from 3 to 9 with little blinding or concealed allocation. Acute injury was defined differently across trials (2 to 10 days), injury grades and sports varied, and most trials compared active programs rather than a true control. The 12-month reinjury estimates come from two studies, and the authors note that the subgroup test was limited by study numbers. The results do not separate the effect of physical modalities from exercise.",
   "practicalImplications":"In the early phase of an acute hamstring injury, a loading program during extensive lengthening can be considered where a faster return to play is the priority, and trunk stabilisation with agility work can be considered where reducing reinjury is the priority. Stretching and physical modalities should not be relied on until better trials exist.",
   "athleteDev":"The study concerns rehabilitation of acute injuries and measures no performance outcomes. Its exercise content, such as eccentric loading during lengthening and trunk and agility work, may inform progressive reconditioning, but the review does not test performance.",
   "rtp":"The loading program is linked with a shorter time to return to play (pooled 28.29 days faster versus the conventional program), so it is the main option supported by this review for return-to-sport planning. Strengthening with trunk and agility work is supported for reducing 12-month reinjury, not for speeding return. The evidence does not cover return-to-sport criteria or RTP testing."

The review reports mainly animal and mechanistic evidence, plus one 17-patient case series of intra-articular BPC-157 injections for tendon and ligament injury with symptom reduction in more than 90% at a minimum of 6 months.    "abstract":"This narrative review summarises the mechanisms, preclinical findings and safety and regulatory issues of therapeutic peptides used in orthopaedic injury and recovery.    "tldr":"Peptides such as BPC-157 and TB-500 show healing effects in animal and mechanistic studies, but human trials are lacking. Most are not approved for orthopaedic use, and sourcing and anti-doping rules need checking before any use.",
   "methods":"Narrative review by three orthopaedic surgeons. No search method, databases, date range or quality appraisal are described. The review groups peptides by function (wound healing, muscle and cartilage repair, sleep and recovery, neuroactive) and discusses mechanisms, safety, sourcing and regulatory status.",
   "findings":"Most evidence is from animal models, mechanistic work and small prospective cohorts or case series. One case series of 17 patients reported reduced symptoms in more than 90% after intra-articular BPC-157 injections for tendon and ligament injuries at a minimum of 6 months. A meta-analysis of six RCTs is cited as showing that AOD-9604 did not change serum IGF-1. The review reports no clinical trials supporting return-to-sport outcomes for any listed peptide, and it notes wide variation in dosing and product quality.",
   "limitations":"No stated search or appraisal methods, so the selection of evidence cannot be reproduced. Most cited evidence is animal or mechanistic, and the review does not grade it.
